questiontext.text: Personalizing the Text: Suffixes and Possession

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 1: Review of Lesson 3

questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lesson 3

Quick Summary

In Lesson 3, we examined the Peal Perfect tense (the suffix conjugation), learning how Syriac describes completed, past actions. The sentence structure shifted from fluidly subject-led (in the present participle) to stringently Verb-Subject-Object (VSO) led narrative chains using the conjunction w- (and).

5-Question Warm-Up Drill

(Answers in Section 9)

  1. What does the suffix -ū indicate on a Perfect verb (e.g., ktabū)?
  2. Translate the basic VSO sentence: Shbaq malkā l-ʾarʿā.
  3. What happens to the pronunciation of k-t-b (ka-tab) in the Syriac 3rd m.sg Perfect?
  4. How do you distinguish between “I went” and “You (m) went” if both are written ܟܬܒܬ (ktabt/ketbet) without vowels?
  5. Translate: w-qreb Yūḥannan.
Warm-up 1. What does the suffix -ū indicate on a Perfect verb (e.g., ktabū)?

generalfeedback.text: The Perfect is the suffix conjugation: person is marked at the end of the verb, and -ū is 3 m.pl.

feedback.text: The 3 f.sg. Perfect ends in -at (ketbat), not -ū.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 2. Translate: Šbaq malkā l-ʾarʿā.

feedback.text: In VSO order the noun right after the verb is the subject; l- marks the object.
Šbaq is Perfect (completed action), so English needs a past tense.

answer.text: The king will leave the earth.

feedback.text: The future/Imperfect is not introduced until Lesson 8; šbaq is Perfect.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 3. What happens to the vowels of k-t-b in the 3rd m.sg. Perfect?

generalfeedback.text: Vowel reduction is a hallmark of Syriac compared with Hebrew and Arabic.

answer.text: The vowel after the first radical drops (vowel reduction), giving ktab.

feedback.text: Right: Syriac reduces the short vowel in the open first syllable, so not *katab but ktab.
Katab is the Hebrew/Arabic shape; Syriac reduces the first vowel.
Prefixes belong to the Imperfect, not the Perfect.

answer.text: The middle radical is doubled, giving kattab.

feedback.text: Doubling marks the Pael stem (Lesson 6), not the Peal Perfect.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 4. Unvocalized ܟܬܒܬ can mean “I wrote” or “you (m) wrote.” How do you tell them apart?

generalfeedback.text: Ambiguous consonantal forms are resolved by context or by vowel points.

answer.text: Only by context or vowel pointing.

feedback.text: Right: the consonants are identical (ketbet vs ktabt).
No extra letter is written; the spelling is the same.
w- means “and” and has nothing to do with person.

answer.text: They cannot be told apart at all.

feedback.text: Readers rely on context, and vocalized texts mark the difference with points.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 5. Translate: w-qreb Yūḥannan.

feedback.text: Qreb is a Perfect verb, not an adjective.

answer.text: And they drew near to Yukhannan.

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 2: Possession and Pronominal Suffixes — Overview

questiontext.text:
Section 2: Possession and Pronominal Suffixes — Overview

In English, we indicate possession using separate pronouns placed before a noun: “my house”, “your king”. In Greek, it’s often an independent genitive pronoun: ὁ οἶκός μου (ho oikos mou).

However, in Semitic languages, possession is expressed by attaching a pronominal suffix directly to the end of the noun.

Cross-Linguistic Comparison: The Possessive Suffix

  • Hebrew: סוּס (sūs, horse) → סוּסִי (sūsī, my horse). אָב (ʾāb, father) → אָבִינוּ (ʾābīnū, our father).
  • Arabic: كتاب (kitāb, book) → كتابي (kitābī, my book).
  • Syriac: ܟܬܒ (ktāb, book) → ܟܬܒܝ (ktāby, my book). ܐܒ (ʾab, father) → ܐܒܘܢ (ʾabūn, our father).

These suffixes are derived from the same ancient roots as the independent pronouns (ʾenā, ʾant, hū) but are highly compressed.

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 3: Pronominal Suffixes on Nouns & Prepositions

questiontext.text:
Section 3: Pronominal Suffixes on Nouns & Prepositions

1. Suffixes on Singular Nouns

To add a suffix, Syriac uses the Absolute state of the noun, not the Emphatic state. (You don’t say “the my-king” *malkā-y; you say “king-my”, malk-y).

  • Malk- (king) + -eh (his) = malkeh (his king).
  • ʾAb- (father) + -y (my) = ʾaby (my father).

2. Suffixes on Prepositions

The exact same suffixes attach to the inseparable prepositions b- (in) and l- (to/for).

  • b- + -eh = beh (in him / in it).
  • l- + -k = lāḵ (to you, m.sg).

3. The Idiom for “To Have”

Syriac (like Hebrew and Arabic) lacks a dedicated verb meaning “to possess” (like English “to have” or Latin “habere”). Instead, Semitic languages use a prepositional phrase: “there is to me” or just “to me”.

  • īt l-y (there-is to-me) → ītly = I have.
  • layt l-eh (there-is-not to-him) = He does not have.
  • ītly srārā = I have truth. (Lit: There is to me truth).

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 4: The Suffix Paradigm for Singular Nouns

questiontext.text:
Section 4: The Suffix Paradigm for Singular Nouns

This paradigm uses the masculine noun malk- (king, root m-l-k) and the feminine noun malkūtt- (kingdom). Notice the suffix column; you must memorize these endings.

Person Suffix Masculine Noun (malk-) Translit Fem Noun (malkūtt-) Translit
1 c.sg. (my) ـܝ (-y) ܡܠܟܝ malk-y ܡܠܟܘܬܝ malkūtt-y
2 m.sg. (your) ـܟ (-k) ܡܠܟܟ malk-āḵ ܡܠܟܘܬܟ malkūtt-āḵ
2 f.sg. (your) ـܟܝ (-ky) ܡܠܟܟܝ malk-ēky ܡܠܟܘܬܟܝ malkūtt-ēky
3 m.sg. (his) ـܗ (-eh) ܡܠܟܗ malk-eh ܡܠܟܘܬܗ malkūtt-eh
3 f.sg. (her) ـܗ (-āh) ܡܠܟܗ malk-āh ܡܠܟܘܬܗ malkūtt-āh
1 c.pl. (our) ـܢ (-n) ܡܠܟܢ malk-an ܡܠܟܘܬܢ malkūtt-an
2 m.pl. (your) ـܟܘܢ (-kūn) ܡܠܟܟܘܢ malk-kūn ܡܠܟܘܬܟܘܢ malkūtt-kūn
2 f.pl. (your) ـܟܝܢ (-kēn) ܡܠܟܟܝܢ malk-kēn ܡܠܟܘܬܟܝܢ malkūtt-kēn
3 m.pl. (their) ـܗܘܢ (-hūn) ܡܠܟܗܘܢ malk-hūn ܡܠܟܘܬܗܘܢ malkūtt-hūn
3 f.pl. (their) ـܗܝܢ (-hēn) ܡܠܟܗܝܢ malk-hēn ܡܠܟܘܬܗܝܢ malkūtt-hēn

Orthography Note: The 3rd masculine singular (-eh) and 3rd feminine singular (-āh) are both spelled with a final Heh (ܗ). Only vowel pointing or context distinguishes “his” from “her”.

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 5: Prepositional "To Have" Paradigm (l- + Suffix)

questiontext.text:
Section 5: Prepositional "To Have" Paradigm (l- + Suffix)

How to say “I have”, “You have”, “He has”, etc., by attaching suffixes to the l- preposition, often preceded by īt (there is).

Person Estrangela (l- + suffix) Transliteration Meaning
1 c.sg. ܠܝ lī to me (I have)
2 m.sg. ܠܟ lāḵ to you (You have)
2 f.sg. ܠܟܝ lēky to you (You have)
3 m.sg. ܠܗ lēh to him (He has)
3 f.sg. ܠܗ lāh to her (She has)
1 c.pl. ܠܢ lān to us (We have)
2 m.pl. ܠܟܘܢ lḵūn to you (You all have)
3 m.pl. ܠܗܘܢ lhūn to them (They have)

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 7: The Story — Part 4

questiontext.text:
Section 7: The Story — Part 4

A Dialogue at the Gate

Narrative note: Watch how the guards use suffixes with prepositions (lēh, lḵūn) and nouns (ʾabūk, ʾemāḵ) to interrogate Yukhannan about his origins and possessions.

Sentence 1

ܩܡ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܒܬܪܥܐ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ qām Yūḥannan b-tarʿā d-malkūttā. qām (stood) Yūḥannan (John) b-tarʿā (in-the-gate) d-malkūttā (of-the-kingdom). → Yukhannan stood at the gate of the kingdom.

Sentence 2

ܘܐܡܪܝܢ ܩܫܝܫܐ ܕܬܪܥܐ ܠܗ w-ʾāmrīn qašīšē d-tarʿā l-ēh: w-ʾāmrīn (and-are-saying) qašīšē (the-elders/guards) d-tarʿā (of-the-gate) l-ēh (to-him): → And the guards of the gate say to him:

Sentence 3

ܡܢ ܐܝܢܐ ܐܬܪܐ ܐܢܬ men ʾaynā ʾatrā ʾant? men (from) ʾaynā (what) ʾatrā (country/place) ʾant (you-[are])? → “From what country are you?”

Sentence 4

ܘܐܝܟܘ ܐܒܘܟ ܘܐܡܟ w-ʾaykō ʾab-ūḵ w-ʾem-āḵ? w-ʾaykō (and-where) ʾab-ūḵ (father-your) w-ʾem-āḵ (and-mother-your)? → “And where is your father and your mother?”

Sentence 5

ܘܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܟ ܒܐܝܕܟ w-mā īt lāḵ b-ʾīd-āḵ? w-mā (and-what) īt (there-is) lāḵ (to-you) b-ʾīd-āḵ (in-hand-your)? → “And what do you have in your hand?”

Sentence 6

ܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ ܝܘܚܢܢ ʾemar l-hūn Yūḥannan: ʾemar (said) l-hūn (to-them) Yūḥannan (John): → Yukhannan said to them:

Sentence 7

ܐܠܗܐ ܗܘ ܐܒܝ ܘܐܪܥܐ ܗܝ ܐܡܝ Alāhā hū ʾab-y, w-ʾarʿā hī ʾem-y. Alāhā (God) hū (he-[is]) ʾab-y (father-my), w-ʾarʿā (and-the-earth) hī (she-[is]) ʾem-y (mother-my). → “God is my father, and the earth is my mother.”

Sentence 8

ܘܠܝܬ ܠܝ ܠܒܘܫܐ ܒܝܫܐ w-layt lī lbūšā bīšā. w-layt (and-there-is-not) lī (to-me) lbūšā (a-garment) bīšā (evil). → “And I do not have an evil garment.”

Sentence 9

ܢܘܗܪܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܒܐܝܕܝ nūhrā d-Alāhā īt-awhy b-ʾīd-y. nūhrā (the-light) d-Alāhā (of-God) īt-awhy (it-is) b-ʾīd-y (in-hand-my). → “The light of God is in my hand.”
Exercise 1. Identify the possessor in ܡܠܟܢ (malk-an).
Exercise 1. Identify the possessor in ܒܝܬܗ (bayt-eh).

generalfeedback.text: ܗ alone can also be 3 f.sg. -āh “her”; the vocalization -eh makes it “his.”

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Identify the possessor in ܐܝܕܟܝ (ʾīd-ēky).

feedback.text: 2 m.sg. is ܟ alone (-āḵ), with no final Yodh.

questiontext.text: Exercise 1. Identify the possessor in ܡܠܟܘܬܗܘܢ (malkūtt-hūn).
Exercise 2. Using l- + suffix: “To you (f.sg).”
Exercise 2. “We have” (“there is to us”).

feedback.text: Layt is the negative: “we do not have.”

questiontext.text: Exercise 2. “He does not have” (“there is not to him”).

feedback.text: Possession is negated with layt, not with bare lā.

questiontext.text: Exercise 2. “To them (m.pl).”
Exercise 3. Translate: ʾAbī ṭābā hū, w-ʾemī ṭābtā hī.

answer.text: My father is good, and my mother is good.

feedback.text: Right: verbless clauses with hū/hī as copula.

answer.text: His father is good, and his mother is good.
My father is a king, and my mother is a queen.
My father was good, and my mother was good.

feedback.text: The pronoun copula gives a present “is.”

questiontext.text: Exercise 3. Translate: Šbaqū talmīdē l-baythūn.
Exercise 3. Translate: Īt lān nūhrā rabbā.

feedback.text: Right: literally “there is to us a great light.”

answer.text: We do not have a great light.

questiontext.text: Exercise 3. Translate: Qālā d-malkā b-ʾarʿan.

answer.text: The voice of the king is in our land.
The voice of the king is in his land.
The king’s word is in our land.
Our king’s voice is in the land.

feedback.text: The suffix is on ʾarʿā, not on malkā.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. Render into Syriac: “My brother is writing a word.”

feedback.text: Ktab is Perfect “wrote”; “is writing” needs the participle.
Kātbā is the feminine participle; “brother” is masculine.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. “The king and his son are going to his kingdom.”

feedback.text: Right: plural participle ʾāzlīn for a compound subject.
ʾEzal is Perfect “went”; “are going” needs the participle.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. “What is in your (m.sg) hand?”
Exercise 4. “We do not have an evil king.”
Exercise 5 (Section 7). Under what three topics does the guard interrogate Yukhannan?

answer.text: Origin (what country), family (where are his father and mother), and possessions (what is in his hand)
His name, his teacher, and his god

feedback.text: Re-read Section 7: the questions are country, parents and possessions.

answer.text: His language, his books, and his journey
His age, his work, and his house

questiontext.text: Exercise 5. Who does Yukhannan claim as his parents?

feedback.text: Not in this story; re-read Section 7.

questiontext.text: Exercise 5. What does Yukhannan explicitly say he does not have?

Section 10: Grammatical Summary

THE PRONOMINAL SUFFIXES (ATTACH TO NOUNS AND PREPOSITIONS)

Suffix Meaning Example (bayt- house) Example (l- to)
-y my baytī (my house) lī (to me)
-k your (m) baytāḵ (your house) lāḵ (to you)
-ky your (f) baytēky (your house) lēky (to you)
-eh his bayteh (his house) lēh (to him)
-āh her baytāh (her house) lāh (to her)
-an our baytan (our house) lān (to us)
-kūn your (pl) baytkūn (your house) lḵūn (to you all)
-hūn their (pl) baythūn (their house) lhūn (to them)

SAYING “TO HAVE” (Possession Formula)

Formula Syriac Meaning
ĪT + L- + Suffix īt lī / ītly I have (There is to me)
LAYT + L- + Suffix layt lēh He does not have
ĪT + L- + Suffix īt lhūn malkā They have a king
